title: Quintus: Two-round Good-case Information Theoretic BFT for $n=5f+1$
authors: Chenyang Liu, Dahlia Malkhi, Kartik Nayak, and Nibesh Shrestha
abstract:
We present, Quintus, information-theoretic BFT protocols for tolerating $f < n/5$ Byzantine faults among $n$ parties. We present two protocols:
 
      (1) The first protocol, Quintus-Fixed, is in a fixed view regime where views advance at a cadence $3\Delta$ time. This protocol incurs a good-case latency of $2\delta$ time where $\delta$ indicates actual network delay and message complexity of $O(n^3)$ in a view. % In optimistic cases with good leaders, it incurs $O(n^2)$ message complexity.

      (2) The second protocol, Quintus-Responsive, is an optimistically responsive protocol with good-case latency of $2\delta$ time, $O(n^2)$ message complexity, and $2\Delta + 2\delta$ worst-case view latency where $\Delta$ denotes a pessimistic network delay parameter under synchrony.

CHENYANG LIU, Duke University, USA
DAHLIA MALKHI, University of California, Santa Barbara, USA
KARTIK NAYAK, Duke University, USA
NIBESH SHRESTHA, Supra Research, USA
We present, Quintus, information-theoretic BFT protocols for tolerating 𝑓 < 𝑛/5 Byzantine faults among 𝑛 parties. We present two
protocols:

     (1) The first protocol, Quintus-Fixed, is in a fixed view regime where views advance at a cadence 3Δ time. This protocol incurs a
          good-case latency of 2𝛿 time where 𝛿 indicates actual network delay and message complexity of 𝑂 (𝑛 3 ) in a view.
     (2) The second protocol, Quintus-Responsive, is an optimistically responsive protocol with good-case latency of 2𝛿 time, 𝑂 (𝑛 2 )
          message complexity, and 2Δ + 2𝛿 worst-case view latency where Δ denotes a pessimistic network delay parameter under
          synchrony.



1    Introduction
Byzantine consensus is a fundamental building block of fault-tolerant distributed systems and blockchains. In the
partially synchronous model, classical results show that consensus can be achieved among 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1 parties despite up
to 𝑓 Byzantine faults [12]. Modern protocols typically rely on digital signatures and quorum certificates to transfer
evidence of previous decisions across “views”. Using these approaches, they primarily optimize three key metrics:
good-case latency, i.e., the time to commit a block when proposed by an honest “leader” and the network is synchronous,
the worst-case view latency, i.e., the worst-case time after GST between the last party entering a view to all parties
entering the next view, and message complexity, which is the number of messages sent by honest parties in a view.
    In the presence of signatures, these protocols with 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1 are able to obtain the optimal good-case latency of
3-rounds1 [3], a message complexity of 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) while requiring worst-case view latency of 3Δ +𝛿 where Δ is a pessimistic
network delay parameter that is respected for all messages when the network is synchronous [7, 11, 20, 21], and 𝛿
represents the actual network delay. On the other hand, when tolerating 𝑛 = 5𝑓 + 1, these protocols achieve a good-case
latency of 2-rounds [10, 14, 16, 18, 21], 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) message complexity while requiring a worst-case latency of 2Δ + 𝛿 [10].
    Motivated by growing interest in both scaling down computational overhead and in removing reliance on digital
signatures that may not be post-quantum secure, recent work has revisited the design of information-theoretic/signature-
free Byzantine consensus protocols under partial synchrony [1, 2, 5, 11, 20, 22–24]. These protocols replace cryptographic
certificates with communication-based mechanisms, relying on authenticated channels to disseminate the state of the
protocol. Prior known information-theoretic protocols operate at the optimal resilience of 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1, and incur a
3-round good-case latency, which is known to be optimal when tolerating 𝑓 < 𝑛/3 faults [1, 2, 11, 24], and the best
known protocol incurs a worst-case latency of 3Δ + 2𝛿 [2].
    In this work, we ask whether we can obtain information-theoretic protocols with 2-round good-case latency for 𝑛 = 5𝑓 +1
while simultaneously minimizing worst-case view latency and message complexity?

    We answer this question affirmatively. We present two protocols, Quintus-Fixed and Quintus-Responsive, in two
different regimes. The first regime is a “fixed view” regime where start times and end times of a view are fixed in
advance and known to all parties. This regime is adopted by several practical blockchains such as Solana [16] and
Ethereum [8]. The second regime is an “optimistically responsive” regime where the time spent in a view can change
depending on network conditions and adversarial behavior. This regime is adopted by several practical blockchains
such as Monad [15] and Espresso Systems [17].

Quintus-Fixed. Our first contribution is a protocol in the fixed view regime that proceeds through three phases of
proposal, voting, and a state dissemination phase in each view. The protocol achieves 2-round good-case latency, a
3-round view, and incurs message and communication complexity of 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) per view. More formally, our protocol
obtains the following result:

    Theorem 1 (Quintus-Fixed). Assuming clocks are synchronized across parties, there exists an information-theoretic,
deterministic, partially synchronous Byzantine broadcast protocol among 𝑛 parties that tolerates 𝑓 Byzantine faults for
𝑛 = 5𝑓 + 1 in a fixed-view regime, that achieves a good-case latency of 2𝛿, has a view duration of 3Δ, and requires 𝑂 (𝑛 2 )
message complexity per view.

Quintus-Responsive. Our second contribution is an optimistically responsive protocol that advances at the speed of
the network. Thus, instead of starting views at predetermined intervals, parties advance views earlier when messages
from previous views arrive sooner. Such protocols tend to outperform fixed view protocols when the actual network
delay 𝛿 ≪ Δ. Quintus-Responsive achieves good-case 2-round latency, with 2Δ + 2𝛿 worst-case latency, and incurs a
message complexity of 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ). More formally, we show:

    Theorem 2 (Quintus-Responsive). There exists an information-theoretic, deterministic, partially synchronous Byzan-
tine broadcast protocol among 𝑛 parties that tolerates 𝑓 Byzantine faults with 𝑛 = 5𝑓 + 1. The protocol achieves a good-case
latency of 2𝛿, worst-case latency of 2Δ + 2𝛿, incurs 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) message complexity, is optimistically responsive, and incurs
optimistic 2𝛿 latency between views.

2   Preliminaries
We consider a system of 𝑛 parties (𝑃1, . . . , 𝑃𝑛 ) consisting of parties, where up to 𝑓 < 𝑛/5 parties may be Byzantine.
Byzantine parties can behave arbitrarily. A party that remains fault-free throughout the execution and follows the
protocol correctly is referred to as honest.
    We assume the partial synchrony model introduced by Dwork et al. [13]. In this model, the system begins in
an asynchronous state during which the adversary can arbitrarily delay messages between honest parties. After an
unknown point in time, known as the Global Stabilization Time (GST), the network becomes partially synchronous: all
messages sent by honest parties are guaranteed to be delivered within a fixed delay Δ. We use 𝛿 to denote the actual
(and possibly variable) message transmission delays, and note that 𝛿 ≤ Δ after GST. Furthermore, we assume that
parties’ local clocks exhibit no drift but may have arbitrary skew.

    Definition 1 (Partially Synchronous Byzantine Broadcast [4]). A partially synchronous Byzantine broadcast
protocol provides the following properties.
• Agreement. If two honest parties commit values 𝑚 and 𝑚 ′ respectively, then 𝑚 = 𝑚 ′ .
• Validity. If the designated broadcaster is honest and GST= 0, then all honest parties commit the broadcaster’s value.

3    Quintus-Fixed: A Fixed View 5𝑓 + 1-Protocol

Protocol Description. Figure 1 presents a signature-free partially synchronous Byzantine broadcast protocol for
𝑛 = 5𝑓 + 1 parties. The protocol relies only on authenticated channels and does not require threshold signatures, quorum
certificates, or any cryptographic aggregation mechanism. The protocol proceeds in views where each view requires
three rounds and thus, runs in 3Δ time, assuming parties have synchronized clocks.
    Each party maintains a local variable S and a local variable key. The key represents the value currently supported
by the party, which stores the value recently voted for in any view.
    The proposal phase of view 𝑉 starts at time 3𝑉 Δ. The designated leader checks if it has received at least 𝑛 − 𝑓 status
messages from the previous view 𝑉 − 1 for 𝑉 ≥ 1. If it has not, then the leader does not propose a value. If it has, then

among these notifications, if a non-⊥ value appears at least 2𝑓 + 1 times, the leader proposes such a value; otherwise, it
may propose any value.
    In the vote phase (3𝑉 Δ + 𝛿), upon receiving the first proposal, parties first process the status messages it received
from the previous view to decide whether to vote for the proposal. If the party receives 2𝑓 + 1 status messages among
≥ 𝑛 − 𝑓 received status messages matching the value leader sent or for ⊥, the party can vote for the proposal. After
voting, the party updates its key accordingly and broadcasts a notify message on the key (3𝑉 + 1)Δ.
    In the commit phase, a value is committed once a party receives 𝑛 − 𝑓 = 4𝑓 + 1 votes for that value in the current
view.
    Moreover, if each party received 𝑛 − 𝑓 notify messages for the current view by 2Δ into the view, it will broadcast
the status message for view change. Once a party see 2𝑓 + 1 notify messages on the same value, it sends a status
on that value; otherwise, it sends a status on ⊥.
    Finally, at any time, upon receiving 𝑓 + 1 (status, 𝑣, 𝑉 ) messages, a party amplifies the message.

Key Intuition. Observe that safety holds within a view since any two sets of 𝑛 − 𝑓 votes intersect in more than one
value. Safety holds across views since, once a value 𝑣 has been committed in a view, there exists a set of 𝑛 − 2𝑓 = 3𝑓 + 1
honest parties who have their key set to 𝑣. Subsequently, no key 𝑣 ′ ≠ 𝑣 can be notified by > 2𝑓 parties, and thus, no
honest party will send a status for 𝑣 ′ ≠ 𝑣. Due to this, no honest party observes 2𝑓 + 1 status on 𝑣 ′ ≠ 𝑣 in subsequent
views and will not vote on an equivocating value.
    Liveness requires all honest parties to vote on an honest leader’s proposal after GST. In particular, if the leader of
view 𝑉 is honest, then we show that this holds so far as GST ≤ (3(𝑉 − 1) + 1)Δ. Observe that, since the network is
synchronous, all honest parties notify and status messages will be received by all honest parties. Among the ≥ 𝑛 − 𝑓
notify messages received by an honest party, at least one of the two status sending conditions must hold. Moreover,
since every party receives every honest notify, there exists at least one condition that holds for all honest parties.
Consequently, all honest parties will send at least one status message, allowing an honest leader to propose.
    Observe that, since a leader proposes based on 2𝑓 + 1 matching status messages, at least 𝑓 + 1 of these are from
honest parties, and the status amplification step ensures that all honest parties amplify this status. This ensures that all
honest parties receive sufficiently many status messages on the value proposed by the leader. Thus, they will all vote
for the leader’s proposal and commit the value.

Latency and message complexity. The protocol incurs a good-case latency [3] of 2-rounds (2𝛿), since a value can be
committed as soon as it is proposed and voted on when the leader is honest and 𝐺𝑆𝑇 = 0.
    The total message complexity per view is 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ). The proposal step requires only 𝑂 (𝑛) communication. Sending the
vote, notify, and status message incurs 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) communication — each of the 𝑛 parties multicast constant number of
such messages.

4     Quintus-Responsive: A Responsive Protocol for 𝑛 = 5𝑓 + 1
We present an information-theoretic responsive partially synchronous Byzantine broadcast protocol in the 𝑛 = 5𝑓 + 1
setting in Figure 2. At a high level, the protocol follows a similar reasoning sketch as in the previous section but allows
for optimistically responsive view changes, and a worst-case view latency of 2Δ + 2𝛿.

4.1    Protocol description
The protocol proceeds in numbered views, each associated with a designated leader. Every view consists of a normal-case
agreement phase followed by a view change phase.
    Each party maintains two local variables: the current view curview, initially 0, and a key key, initially ⊥. The key
stores the value most recently voted for in any view and is used during the view change phase.

Normal-case agreement. To initiate view 𝑉 , the leader waits until receiving 2𝑓 + 1 identical attest messages or
3𝑓 + 1 identical vote messages from view 𝑉 − 1. These messages summarize the state until the previous view. If they
identify a value 𝑥 ≠ ⊥, the leader proposes 𝑣 = 𝑥; otherwise, it may propose any value 𝑣. The leader then broadcasts a
(propose, 𝑣, 𝑉 ) message (line 1). The leader also starts a timer of 2Δ when it enters the view.
    Upon receiving the proposal, a party votes only if it is still in view 𝑉 (timer for the view 𝑉 was set and does not
expire), the proposal is compatible with the set of view (𝑉 − 1)-attest messages it received, i.e., either 3𝑓 + 1 attest
messages on the proposed value or on ⊥, and if the party has not voted before in this view. The party records 𝑣 as its
current key and broadcasts a (vote, 𝑣, 𝑉 ) message (line 3). A party also votes if it observes 𝑓 + 1 (vote, 𝑣, 𝑉 ) messages,
if the party has not sent a vote or attest or timeout on an equivocating value in view 𝑉 or higher (line 4).
    A party commits a value once it collects 𝑛 − 𝑓 matching vote messages (line 5).

4.2     Key Intuition

Safety and Liveness. Observe that safety follows based on quorum intersection arguments within and across views. If
a party commits on a value 𝑣 in view 𝑉 , it obtains 𝑛 − 𝑓 votes, and thus, 𝑛 − 2𝑓 honest votes. Any two such 𝑛 − 2𝑓
honest sets intersect in 2𝑓 + 1 > 0 honest parties who will not vote on equivocating values. Across views, once a party
commits 𝑣, at least 𝑛 − 2𝑓 ≥ 3𝑓 + 1 honest parties will have their key set to 𝑣. Subsequently, no other value, including ⊥
can obtain 2𝑓 + 1 attest messages in the next view, and inductively, in any subsequent view. Due to this, no honest
party votes on any other value in subsequent views. We note that, to ensure liveness, there is an indirect voting rule that

allows parties to vote based on 𝑓 + 1 votes if they have not sent a conflicting vote, attest, or timeout message but this
requires a first honest party to send one of these messages, which will not happen once a value has been committed.
    For liveness, we need to ensure that a value that is proposed by an honest leader after GST will be committed. First,
once an honest party enters a view after GST, other honest parties enter the view soon enough. In particular, observe
that, once a non-leader party enters a view, it enters based on receiving 3𝑓 + 1 attest messages or 4𝑓 + 1 vote messages
for the same value, and thus, all honest parties will obtain 2𝑓 + 1 attest or 3𝑓 + 1 vote messages within Δ time. The
leader can enter the view at this time. For other parties, the attest messages will be amplified within another Δ time.
Similarly, if the leader enters based on a view based on 2𝑓 + 1 attest or 3𝑓 + 1 vote messages, by similar reasoning,
due to amplification, then all honest parties enter the view within 2Δ time. Thus, if some honest party moves to a higher
view, all other parties will follow soon enough.
    Second, to ensure that parties do not stay stuck in the same view, we require parties to all send a vote or timeout
message within the view. Among these, if the same value appears 2𝑓 + 1 times, then parties send an attest for it,
and on obtaining 2𝑓 + 1 such attest messages, parties can move to the next view. If no value appears 2𝑓 + 1 times,
then parties send an attest on ⊥, and parties can move to the next view on collecting 2𝑓 + 1 attest on ⊥ messages.
Importantly, since there exist 4𝑓 + 1 honest attest messages, it ensures that at least one of these cases is triggered, and
all parties can move to the next view after GST.
    Finally, after GST, we need to ensure that parties vote on an honest leader’s proposal. Since the leader enters within
Δ time of any honest party, they will not time out of the view before receiving the proposal because of the 2Δ timer.
Thus, if they are still in the view, the leader’s view entry condition ensures the requirements for voting are met, and
they will directly vote for the leader’s proposal. The only remaining scenario is if an honest party has already moved to
a higher view before voting. This is because they either observed 3𝑓 + 1 attest or 4𝑓 + 1 vote messages for the same
value. In either case, this implies at least 𝑓 + 1 honest parties have voted, and thus, the party will vote indirectly with
the caveat that it has not voted, sent timeout on, or sent attest on an equivocating value in a higher view. Note that
this cannot happen because 2𝑓 + 1 attest on an equivocating message can never be formed in view 𝑉 (leader is honest,
and we are after GST) and, thus, in any subsequent views. Thus, an honest party will not vote on an equivocating value
in a higher view after GST.

Latency. Observe that the protocol has a good-case latency of 2𝛿. When GST = 0, and the leader is honest, all honest
parties will vote on the leader’s proposal, and 𝑛 − 𝑓 votes will be generated within 2𝛿 time at all honest parties.
    In addition, the worst-case view latency is the time between the last honest party entering a view to all honest
parties entering the next view. Suppose the last honest party enters a view at time 𝑡. Then, by time 𝑡 + 2Δ, all honest
parties will have sent a vote or timeout message. By time 𝑡 + 2Δ + 𝛿, every honest party would have received a vote
or timeout for every honest party. At this point, either some value will appear 2𝑓 + 1 times or no value will appear
2𝑓 + 1 times. Thus, every party will send the same attest message, which will arrive at all parties within 𝛿 time. Thus,
the worst-case latency is 2Δ + 2𝛿 time.
    Finally, in good cases, i.e., when consecutive leaders are honest, and after GST, parties switch between views in 2𝛿
time since parties can enter the next view based on a quorum of vote messages.

Message complexity. Observe that, for every step of the protocol, every party sends 𝑂 (1) messages to all other parties.
In particular, since an attest message on 𝑥 ≠ ⊥ relies on the existence of 2𝑓 + 1 and thus, 𝑓 + 1 honest, vote or
timeout messages, an honest party can attest only 𝑂 (1) messages in a view. Thus, the message complexity of the
protocol is 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) per view.

then the sender of that timeout message must have had curview = 𝑉 − 1 when its timer expired; hence, that honest
party must already have entered view 𝑉 − 1.
     In the third case, where the attest message is sent by amplification, the party received 𝑓 + 1 attest messages for
view 𝑉 − 1. Since at most 𝑓 parties are Byzantine, at least one of these attest messages was sent earlier by an honest
party. Therefore, it must have been sent by one of the first two attest-generation rules which implies that some honest
party had already entered view 𝑉 − 1.
     Therefore, the claim follows.                                                                                          □

     Lemma 6. If 𝑙𝑉 is honest and proposes value 𝑣 in view 𝑉 at time 𝑡 ≥ 𝐺𝑆𝑇 , then no honest party sends (attest, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or
(vote, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or (timeout, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) for any value 𝑣 ′ ≠ 𝑣, including ⊥, in any view 𝑊 ≥ 𝑉 .

     Proof. We prove this by contradiction. Let 𝑊 ≥ 𝑉 be the first view in which some honest party sends a conflicting
message, either (vote, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or (attest, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or (timeout, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) for some value 𝑣 ′ ≠ 𝑣. Let 𝑚 be the first conflicting
message by an honest party in the causal order.
     We consider all possible ways in which such a message could be sent.
     Consider a message 𝑚 = (vote, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ). If 𝑊 = 𝑉 , then this is impossible through the direct voting rule because the
leader 𝑙𝑉 is honest and proposes only 𝑣. Thus, an honest party can directly vote only for 𝑣 in view 𝑉 . Moreover, vote
amplification cannot trigger an honest party to send (vote, 𝑣 ′, 𝑉 ): to send (vote, 𝑣 ′, 𝑉 ) by amplification, an honest
party must receive 𝑓 + 1 (vote, 𝑣 ′, 𝑉 ) messages. Since at most 𝑓 parties are Byzantine, at least one of these votes must
have been sent by an honest party by direct voting rule, contradicting the choice of 𝑚.

  Now suppose 𝑊 > 𝑉 . If an honest party directly votes for 𝑣 ′ in view 𝑊 , then it must have received a proposal
(propose, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) and 3𝑓 + 1 (attest, 𝑥,𝑊 − 1) messages for some 𝑥 ∈ {𝑣 ′, ⊥}. Since 𝑣 ′ ≠ 𝑣, we have 𝑥 ≠ 𝑣. Among
these 3𝑓 + 1 attest messages, at least 2𝑓 + 1 are sent by honest parties. Hence, some honest party must have previously
sent (attest, 𝑥,𝑊 − 1) with 𝑥 ≠ 𝑣, contradicting the minimality of 𝑊 as the first view in which an honest party sends
a conflicting message. Similarly, vote amplification cannot produce (vote, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ), because receiving 𝑓 + 1 votes for 𝑣 ′
requires at least one prior honest vote for 𝑣 ′ , contradicting the choice of 𝑚.
  Second, suppose 𝑚 = (timeout, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ). By the timeout rule, the sender has not voted in view 𝑊 and sends its current
key. Thus, at the time of sending, the party has key = 𝑣 ′ .
  For 𝑊 = 𝑉 , this is impossible since 𝑙𝑉 is honest and every honest party receives the honest leader’s proposal and
corresponding view 𝑉 − 1 attest message before its timer expires and therefore votes for 𝑣 before it can send a timeout
in view 𝑉 .
  For 𝑊 > 𝑉 , observe that key is updated only when an honest party votes. Since the party’s key is set to 𝑣 ′ at the
time it sends (timeout, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ), either it never voted for 𝑣 after the honest proposal in view 𝑉 , or it previously voted for
𝑣 ′ . The second case contradicts the choice of 𝑚.
  The first case is impossible. Every honest party receives the honest leader’s proposal and corresponding view 𝑉 − 1
attest message before its timer expires and votes for 𝑣 and therefore votes for 𝑣, or it advances before voting in view
𝑉 . This advancement can only be caused by votes for 𝑣 which triggers vote amplification for 𝑣.
  We now consider the case where 𝑚 = (attest, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) was sent. An honest party can send such an attest message
in one of three ways.
  First, the party may receive 𝑛 − 𝑓 messages for view 𝑊 , each of which is either a vote or a timeout message, such
that no value appears at least 2𝑓 + 1 times. Since 𝑚 is the first conflicting message, every honest vote or timeout
message for view 𝑊 sent before 𝑚 is for 𝑣. Among the 𝑛 − 𝑓 received messages, at most 𝑓 are Byzantine, so at least
3𝑓 + 1 are honest messages for 𝑣. Therefore, 𝑣 appears at least 3𝑓 + 1, and in particular at least 2𝑓 + 1, times among the
received messages. Hence, the condition for sending (attest, ⊥,𝑊 ) is not satisfied.
  Second, the party may receive 2𝑓 + 1 messages for the same value 𝑣 ′ , each of which is either a (vote, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or a
(timeout, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) message. Since at most 𝑓 parties are Byzantine, at least 𝑓 + 1 of these messages are from honest parties.
Therefore, some honest party must have previously sent either (vote, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or (timeout, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ), contradicting the
choice of 𝑚.
  Third, the party may send (attest, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) by attest amplification after receiving 𝑓 + 1 messages of the form
(attest, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ). Since at most 𝑓 parties are Byzantine, at least one of these attest messages must have been sent
earlier by an honest party, contradicting the choice of 𝑚.
  Thus every possible way of producing the first conflicting honest message leads to a contradiction. Therefore, no
honest party sends (vote, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or (attest, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) or (timeout, 𝑣 ′,𝑊 ) for any 𝑣 ′ ≠ 𝑣 and any view 𝑊 ≥ 𝑉 .            □

     Information-Theoretic BFT. Table 1 summarizes representative information-theoretic BFT protocols and their latency,
communication, and responsiveness guarantees. PBFT [11] was the first signature-free BFT protocol to achieve the
optimal good-case latency of 3𝛿 under 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1 and an 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) message complexity.

  Information-Theoretic HotStuff (IT-HS) [5, 23] adapts HotStuff to the signature-free setting. The simplified blog
construction [23] achieves 4𝛿 good-case latency and 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) message complexity by using a boosting mechanism to
ensure totality of accept messages during view change. However, it is not responsive: the leader must wait 2Δ to
collect suggested locks from all honest parties. The paper version [5] replaces this fixed wait with a three-key quorum
mechanism, restoring responsiveness at the cost of two additional rounds on the critical path and thus 6𝛿 good-case
latency.
  TetraBFT [24] achieves responsive consensus with 5𝛿 good-case latency, 10Δ view length, and 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) message
complexity. Rather than relying on lock-based safety, it includes prior vote information in view-change messages,
preventing honest parties from echoing unsafe values and eliminating one round relative to IT-HS.
  DispersedSimplex [19, Sec. 7] introduced a signature-free variant by adding the “echo/ready” logic of Bracha’s reliable
broadcast (RBC) to every messages to be sent. This makes all of the latency bounds essentially double (e.g. good-case
latency of 6𝛿) because the every party needs to wait for the amplification of every message to complete.
  Forget-IT [1] is the first responsive signature-free protocol to achieve the optimal 3𝛿 good-case latency under
𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1. Its 7Δ view length is required to support constant storage and responsiveness, but makes view changes
costly under consecutive faulty leaders or asynchronous executions.
  IT-Kuplex [2] is an improvement over Forget-IT in terms of view length, while inheriting other properties. It reduces
the view length, from 4Δ + 3𝛿 to 3Δ + 2𝛿 under 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1 and 3Δ + 𝛿 under 4𝑓 + 1. By assuming synchronized clocks,
IT-Kuplex reduced the entrance gap of Δ by aged quorum. Under 𝑛 = 4𝑓 + 1, due to the fact that quorum size 2𝑓 + 1 is a
majority of 4𝑓 + 1, no two conflicting messages can reach that quorum of the same view, this can reduce one round of
amplification of messages.
  A recent work Simple-IT [25] leverages the optimistic reliable broadcast (RBC) for leaders’ proposal, while a novel
primitive called Reliable Notification (RN) for skipping rounds like in Simplex. By leveraging Opt-RBC [22], Simple-IT
can achieve good-case latency of 5𝛿, 3𝛿 optimistically; by leveraging Bracha-RBC [6], Simple-IT can achieve good-case
latency of 4𝛿.
